readings.c2s4:
¶
'''B.''' ''interrog.'' What? as, ''whatever'' shall I do? [Vulgar, but common in recent British colloquial use.]
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''II.''' ''a. rel.'' Of what kind or sort it may be; no matter what; any or all that: applied to persons and things: as, ''whatever'' person is appointed must be satisfactory to the court.
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll forgive you,
''Whatever'' torment you do put me to.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 1. 84.}}}}
{{smaller block|The knowledge of the theory of logic has no tendency ''whatever'' to make men good reasoners.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whatever'' side he was on, he could always find excellent reasons for it. ''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 36.}}

'''what-like''' (hwot′līk), ''indef. rel. a.'' Of what appearance or character. [Colloq. or provincial.]
{{smaller block|She knows Miss Abbey of old, remind her, and she knows ''what-like'' the home and ''what-like'' the friend is likely to turn out. ''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend, iii. 2.}}

'''Whatman paper.''' See ''paper''.

'''whatna''' (hwot′nä̤), ''a.'' Same as ''whaten.'' [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>There was a lad was born in Kyle,
But ''whatna'' day o’ ''whatna'' style,
I doubt it ’s hardly worth the while
To be sae nice wi’ Robin.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', There was a Lad.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''whatness''' (hwot′nes), ''n.'' [< ''what''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness.''] In ''metaph.'', a quiddity. [Rare.]

'''what-not''' (hwot′not), ''n.'' [< ''what not'' (see ''what''<sup>1</sup>); the stand being so called as used to hold shells, photographs, bric-a-brac, “and ''what not''”: see under ''what''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A stand or set of shelves on which to keep or display small articles of curiosity or ornament, as well as books, papers, etc.; an étagère.
{{smaller block|What cheerfulness those works of art will give to the little parlors up in the country, when they are set up with other shells on the ''what-not'' in the corner!
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Their Pilgrimage, p. 51.}}}}
'''2.''' Anything; no matter what; what you please. See ''what not'', under ''what''<sup>1</sup>, A. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|I profess to be an impartial chronicler of poor Phil’s fortunes, misfortunes, friendships, and ''what-nots.''
{{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, ix.}}}}

'''whatreck''' (hwot′rek), ''adv.'' [Short for ''what reck I?'' ‘what care I?’] Nevertheless. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I wot he was na slaw, man; . . .
But yet, ''what-reck'', he, at Quebec,
Montgomery-like did fa’, man.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', The American War.}}}}

'''whatso†''' (hwot′sō), ''a.'' and ''pron.'' [< ME. ''whatso, whatswa, whatse, hwatse, quat so'', what so, < ''what''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''whoso.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Of whatever character, kind, or sort; no matter what (person or thing): an indefinite relative use.
{{smaller block|''What'' man ''so'' vs metes may vs sone knowe.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2565.}}}}

'''II.''' ''pron.'' No matter what or who; whatsoever; whosoever.
readings.c3s4:
{{smaller block|<poem>For, ’tis not Courage (''whatsoe’r'' men say),
But Cowardize, to make ones Self away.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Trophies.}}}}

'''whatsom†''', ''a.'' and ''pron.'' Same as ''whatsomever.''

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|what|6887|whatsom}}</noinclude>{{nop}}(''b'') What sort of; such . . . as.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thorow his prayer they may be clensed of synne
''What'' tyme they entre the chapelle with-In.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 126.}}}}
{{smaller block|Anno 1476, at ''what'' time the Switzers took their revenge upon Charles Duke of Burgundie. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 42.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And heavenly quires the hymenæan sung,
''What'' day the genial angel to our sire
Brought her, in naked beauty.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 712.}}}}
{{smaller block|Now a merchant may wear ''what'' boots he pleases.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Book of Snobs, xiii.}}}}
(''c'') Any who or which; whatever; whoever.
{{smaller block|Also ''qwat'' brother or sustre die, and he may noughte be broughte . . . wyt his owne catelle, he sal be broughte wyt the broderhedes. {{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 110.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I love thee not a jar o’ the clock behind
''What'' lady-she her lord. ''Shak.'', W. T., i. 2. 44.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|I never said aught but this, That ''what'' rule, or laws, or custom, or people were flat against the word of God are diametrically opposite to Christianity.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}
(''d'') How much. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|When a man bets he doesn’t well know ''what'' money he uses. {{right|''Trollope'', Last Chronicle of Barset, xxxvii.}}}}

'''But what''', but that; but who; who or that . . . not.
{{smaller block|There was scarce a farmer’s daughter within ten miles round ''but what'' had found him successful.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Not a writer . . . that mentions his name ''but what'' tells the story of him. {{right|''Bentley'', Diss. on Euripides, § 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|There are few madmen ''but what'' are observed to be afraid of the strait waistcoat.
{{right|''Bentham'', Introd. to Morals and Legislation, xiv. 28, note.}}}}

'''What as†''', that which.
<poem>Here I do bequeathe to thee,
In full possession, half that Kendal hath
And ''what as'' Bradford holds of me in chief.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Old Plays'', II. 47.}}}}

'''What dones†'''   [''what dones'' is literally ‘what made,’ ''dones'' being the genitive of ''don'', E. ''done'', pp. of ''do'', make, used in the genitive in imitation of ''kinnes'' in ''what kinnes'', of what-kind], of what sort; what kind.
{{smaller block|<poem>And whan I seighe it was so slepyng, I went
To warne Pilates wyf ''what dones'' man was Iesus;
For Iuwes hateden hym and han done hym to deth.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xviii. 298.}}}}

'''What that†''', whatsoever; whatever; what. Also ''that what.''
{{smaller block|Him ne dret [dreadeth] naȝt to do zenne, ''huet thet'' hit by [be]. ''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 34.

''What'' lutles [little] ''that'' he et.
{{right|''Poems and Lives of Saints'' (ed. Furnivall), p. 396.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What schulde I telle . . .
And of moche other thing ''what that'' then was?</poem>
{{right|''Rob. of Brunne'', Prol.}}}}
{{smaller block|''What that'' a king himselfe bit [bids].
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., I. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|''That what'' is extremely proper in one company may be highly improper in another.
{{right|''Chesterfield.''}}}}

'''C.''' ''indef.'' (''a'') Something; anything: obsolete except in such colloquial phrases as ''I’ll tell you what'' (by abbreviation for ''what it is, what I think'', or the like).
{{smaller block|<poem>Al was us never broche ne rynge,
Ne ellis ''what'' [var. ''nought'' and ''ought''] fro women sent.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1741.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Wot you ''what'', my lord?
To-day the lords you talk of are beheaded.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 2. 92.}}}}
{{smaller block|I’ll ''tell you what'' now of the devil.
{{right|''Massinger and Dekker'', Virgin-Martyr, iii. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|I ''tell you what''—Ellery Davenport lays out to marry a real angel. He ’s to swear and she ’s to pray!
{{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 518.}}}}

(''b''†) A thing; a portion; an amount; a bit: as, a little ''what.''

{{smaller block|Thanne she a lytel ''what'' smylynge seyde.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iv. prose 6.}}}}

{{smaller block|Then the kynge anone called his seruaunt, that hadde but one lofe and a lytell ''whatte'' of wyne.
{{right|''Fabyan'', Chron., clxxii.}}}}

<poem>They prayd him sit, and gave him for to feed
Such homely ''what'' as serves the simple clowne.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. ix. 7.}}}}

'''To know what ’s what.''' {{smaller|See ''know''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''what<sup>1</sup>''' (hwot), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''what;'' < ''what, pron.'']   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' Why?

<poem>''What'' sholde he studie, and make himselven wood,
Upon a book in cloistre alwey to poure?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 184.}}}}

<poem>''What'' is the shepe to blame in youre syght
Whane he is shorne of his flees & maade alle bare,
Thoughe folke of malyce for her wollis fyght?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 20.}}}}

<poem>Ahlas ''what'' should she fight?
Fewe women win by fight.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Gascoigne'', Philomene (Steele Glas, etc., ed. Arber), p. 97.}}}}

{{smaller block|''What'' should I don this [imperial] robe, and trouble you?
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., i. 1. 189.}}}}

{{smaller block|But ''what'' do we suffer misshaped and enormous prelatism, as we do, thus to blanch and varnish her deformities with the fair colours, as before of martyrdom, so now of episcopacy?
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}

'''2.''' To what degree? in what respect?

{{smaller block|For ''what'' is a man advantaged if he gain the whole world and lose himself?
{{right|Luke ix. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For ''what'' are men better than sheep or goats . . .
If, knowing God, they lift not hands of prayer?</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Passing of Arthur.}}}}

'''3†.''' How; how greatly; to what an extent or degree; how remarkably: exclamatory and intensive.
{{smaller block|O! ''what'' I am fetys and fayre and fygured full fytt!
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|'''What . . . what,''' in some measure; in part; partly by; in consequence of; partly: now followed by ''with'': indefinite and distributive in value.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Lordinges, the tyme wasteth nyght and day,
And steleth from us, ''what'' prively slepinge,
And ''what'' thurgh necligence in our wakinge,
As dooth the streem, that turneth never agayn,
Descending fro the montaigne into playn.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Man of Law’s Tale, l. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Than woot I wele she myghte nevere fayle
For to ben holpen, ''what'' at youre instaunce,
''What with'' hire other frendes generaunce.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 1441.}}}}
{{smaller block|Than sente Gawein aboute to euery garnyson thourgh the reame of Logres, and assembled xxx<sup>mi</sup> ''what'' oon ''what'' other.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 277.}}}}
{{smaller block|Most men, as it happens in this world, either weakly, or falsly principl’d, ''what'' through ignorance, and ''what'' through custom of licence, both in discours and writing, by what hath bin of late written in vulgar, have not seem’d to attain the decision of this point.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|With omission of the second ''what'' (so frequently):}}
{{smaller block|''What'' for hire kynrede and hir nortelrie.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 47.}}}}
{{smaller block|''What with'' pride, projects, and knavery, poor Peter was grown distracted.
{{right|''Swift'', Tale of a Tub, iv.}}}}

'''II.''' ''conj.'' '''1.''' So much as; so far as. {{smaller block|<poem>
Ector, with ful many a bolde baroun,
Cast on a day with Grekes for to fighte,
As he was wont to greve hem ''what'' he myghte.
</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 35.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
To helpe youre freendis ''what'' I may.
</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6300.}}}}
{{smaller block|Mr. Brown, being present, observed them [Indians] to be much affected, and one especially did weep very much, though covered it ''what'' hee could.
{{right|''T. Shepard'', Clear Sunshine of the Gospel, p. 36.}}}}
'''2.''' That. (''a''†) In ''alwhat'', until (compare ''although'', etc.).
{{smaller block|Tho kinges hem wenten and hi seghen [they saw] tho sterre thet yede bi-fore hem. ''al-wat'' hi kam over tho huse war ure louerd was. {{right|''Old Eng. Misc.'' (ed. Morris), p. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thet heaued me akth; ich ne ssel by an eyse [I shall not be at ease] ''al-huet'' ich habbe ydronke.
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 51.}}}}
(''b'') In the phrase ''but what'': but that; that . . . not.
{{smaller block|The Abbot cannot be humbled ''but what'' the community must be humbled in his person. {{right|''Scott'', Monastery, x.}}}}
{{smaller block|Not a thing stolen ''but what'' the sea gave it up.
{{right|''J. H. Newman.''}}}}

'''what<sup>2</sup>†''' (hwot), ''a.''   [< ME. ''hwat'', quick, < AS. ''hwæt'', keen, sharp, bold (= OS. ''hwat'' = Icel. ''hvatr'', keen). Cf. ''whet<sup>1</sup>''.]   Quick; sharp; bold.
{{smaller block|Ther weoren eorles swithe ''whæte''. {{right|''Layamon'', l. 1137.}}}}

'''whatabouts''' (hwot′a-bouts″), ''n.'' The matters which one is about or occupied with. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|You might know of all my goings on, and ''whatabouts'' and whereabouts, from Henry Taylor.
{{right|''Southey'', To G. C. Bedford, March 3, 1830.}}}}

'''what-d’ye-call-it, what-d’ye-call-’em''' (hwot′-dye-kâl′it, -em). A word substituted for the name of a thing, because of forgetfulness or ignorance, or in slight contempt. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|There is no part of the body, an’ please your honour, where a wound occasions more intolerable anguish than upon the knee, . . . there being so many tendons and ''what-d’ye-call-ems'' all about it.
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, viii. 19.}}}}

'''whate’er''' (hwot-ãr′), ''pron.'' A contracted form of ''whatever.''

{{smaller block|He strikes ''whate’er'' is in his way.
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 623.}}}}

'''whaten, whatten''' (hwot′n), ''a.''   [Sc. also ''whatan'', and (with the indef. article) ''whatna''; < ''what''<sup>1</sup> + ''-en'', orig. adj. inflection.]   What; what kind of. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]

{{smaller block|Lord safe us! only look at him sitting asleep. ''Whatan'' a face! {{right|''Noctes Ambrosianæ'', Oct., 1828.}}}}

'''whatever''' (hwot-ev′ėr), ''pron.'' and ''a.''   [< ''what''<sup>1</sup> + ''ever''.]   '''I.''' ''pron.'' '''A.''' ''indef. rel.'' Anything which; no matter what; all that.

<poem>To effect
''Whatever'' I shall happen to devise.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iv. 1. 330.}}}}
<poem>The very best will variously incline,
And what rewards your virtue, punish mine.
''Whatever'' is, is right.   ''Pope'', Essay on Man, iv. 145.</poem>
{{smaller block|The board was expected to make itself thoroughly acquainted with ''whatever'' concerned the colonies.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 9.}}}}

'''B.''' ''interrog.'' What? as, ''whatever'' shall I do? [Vulgar, but common in recent British colloquial use.]

'''II.''' ''a. rel.'' Of what kind or sort it may be; no matter what; any or all that: applied to persons and things: as, ''whatever'' person is appointed must be satisfactory to the court.
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll forgive you,
''Whatever'' torment you do put me to.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 1. 84.}}}}
{{smaller block|The knowledge of the theory of logic has no tendency ''whatever'' to make men good reasoners.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whatever'' side he was on, he could always find excellent reasons for it.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 36.}}}}

'''what-like''' (hwot′līk), ''indef. rel. a.'' Of what appearance or character. [Colloq. or provincial.]
{{smaller block|She knows Miss Abbey of old, remind her, and she knows ''what-like'' the home and ''what-like'' the friend is likely to turn out.
{{right|''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend, iii. 2.}}}}

'''Whatman paper.''' See ''paper''.

'''whatna''' (hwot′nä̤), ''a.'' Same as ''whaten.''   [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>There was a lad was born in Kyle,
But ''whatna'' day o’ ''whatna'' style,
I doubt it ’s hardly worth the while
To be sae nice wi’ Robin.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', There was a Lad.}}}}

'''whatness''' (hwot′nes), ''n.''   [< ''what''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness.'']   In ''metaph.'', a quiddity. [Rare.]

'''what-not''' (hwot′not), ''n.''   [< ''what not'' (see ''what''<sup>1</sup>); the stand being so called as used to hold shells, photographs, bric-a-brac, “and ''what not''”: see under ''what''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A stand or set of shelves on which to keep or display small articles of curiosity or ornament, as well as books, papers, etc.; an étagère.
{{smaller block|What cheerfulness those works of art will give to the little parlors up in the country, when they are set up with other shells on the ''what-not'' in the corner!
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Their Pilgrimage, p. 51.}}}}
'''2.''' Anything; no matter what; what you please. See ''what not'', under ''what''<sup>1</sup>, A. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|I profess to be an impartial chronicler of poor Phil’s fortunes, misfortunes, friendships, and ''what-nots.''
{{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, ix.}}}}

'''whatreck''' (hwot′rek), ''adv.''   [Short for ''what reck I?'' ‘what care I?’]   Nevertheless. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I wot he was na slaw, man; . . .
But yet, ''what-reck'', he, at Quebec,
Montgomery-like did fa’, man.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', The American War.}}}}

'''whatso†''' (hwot′sō), ''a.'' and ''pron.''   [< ME. ''whatso, whatswa, whatse, hwatse, quat so'', what so, < ''what''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''whoso.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Of whatever character, kind, or sort; no matter what (person or thing): an indefinite relative use.
{{smaller block|''What'' man ''so'' vs metes may vs sone knowe.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2565.}}}}

'''II.''' ''pron.'' No matter what or who; whatsoever; whosoever. {{smaller block|<poem>But it were any persone obstinat,
''Whatso'' he were, of heigh or lowe estat,
Him wolde he snibben sharply for the nones.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 522.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“In exitu Israel de Ægypto!”
Thus sang they all together in one voice,
With ''whatso'' in that Psalm is after written.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', tr. of Dante’s Purgatorio, ii.}}}}
Sometimes written as two separate words.
{{smaller block|<poem>Quyt is she
From yow this yer, ''what'' after ''so'' befalle.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 664.}}}}

'''whatsoe’er''' (hwot-sọ̄-ãr′), ''pron.'' A contracted form of ''whatsoever.''

'''whatsoever''' (hwot-sọ̄-ev′ėr), ''a.'' and ''pron.''   [< ME. ''whatsoever''; < ''what''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup> + ''ever''. Cf. ''whatso'' and ''whatsomever.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Of whatever nature, kind, or sort; whatever: an intensive form of ''whatever'', still separable and used as a correlative phrase.
{{smaller block|I have learned in ''whatsoever'' state I am therewith to be content.
{{right|Phil. iv. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Goodness guide thy actions ''whatsoever!''</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'' (?), Faithful Friends, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Meridians, which are Circles passing ouer our heads, in ''what'' part of the World ''soeuer'' we be.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 50.}}}}
{{smaller block|Marauding thieves, to be destroyed by ''whatsoever'' method possible.
{{right|''The Academy'', March 28, 1891, p. 298.}}}}

'''II.''' ''pron.'' What thing or things soever; no matter what thing or things; whatever or whoever.
{{smaller block|I will knowe the soth [truth], ''what-so-euer'' it coste.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|Youth, ''whatsoever'' thou art, thou art but a scurvy fellow.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4. 163.}}}}
<poem>For, ’tis not Courage (''whatsoe’r'' men say),
But Cowardize, to make ones Self away.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Trophies.}}}}

'''whatsom†''', ''a.'' and ''pron.'' Same as ''whatsomever.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
